name: Carla Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carla, thanks for coming. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will have your name on it. So you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you actually think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm a straight talker, my husband says too straight. I'll tell you what I think and you can make of it what you like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Perfect. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the Orchard Fields estate, a hundred and twenty new houses for a mid-sized housebuilder, doing second fix. That's the finishing carpentry once the plaster's dry, hanging doors, skirting boards, architraves, sometimes a staircase. I came into it at forty, after years at home with the kids and cleaning at the primary school, because a friend from church has a husband who's a site manager, and he gave me a chance. I love a door that closes with a soft click first time, it's the best feeling on site. What wears me out is the targets, eight doors a day, and I'm still only managing five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was always more talk than action. I'd say it to the girls at church and to my husband, who'd say he told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I have time to get good at this. I'm slow, I know I'm slow, and I need a few more years before I'm on a full rate. If nothing changes, I'll get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Orchard Fields, get my door count up from five to eight a day, and get my card for the skilled rate. Try to put twenty a week into the savings tin, which is the most we've ever managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really, like when the weather forecast is wrong and it stays dry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you keep track of money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a notebook, every penny, Sunday nights at the kitchen table. Ken's a self-employed roofer, so his money comes in lumps, and mine's steady but small. At the moment we've got about three weeks in the bank and the mortgage takes nearly half of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI at all at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Emi showed me how to ask it to explain her maths homework, so I can help her without looking silly. And once I used it to work out the angle for a staircase handrail, then I checked it with the foreman because I don't trust it completely.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, it was always more talk than action. I'd say it to the women at church and to my husband, who'd say he told me so.
S0.think: It means I have time to get good at this. I'm slow and I need a few more years before I'm on a full rate, but if nothing changes, I'll get there.
S0.do: Keeps working at Orchard Fields, aiming to raise her daily door count from five to eight and earn the skilled rate. Tries to put 20 a week into savings, the most the family has ever managed.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a wrong forecast that leaves the day dry.
S0.quote: In a notebook, every penny, Sunday nights at the kitchen table.
S0.fieldNote: She is an organised planner who keeps the family accounts in a notebook every Sunday. The calm picture gives her what she most needs, which is time to get up to speed. She uses AI occasionally and carefully, and double-checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stop waiting for someone to save them and get on with it. Learn the new things, work hard, and look after your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit worried, because I'm the slowest on the gang. If a machine makes the others faster, they won't need me. But I think finishing work is harder for machines than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the others on site start using the new tools, I'd learn them too, and I'd ask Emi to help me with anything on the phone. I'd try to save a bit more each month, maybe thirty a week if Ken has a good summer. And I'd ask the foreman what the firm wants us to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a tooth that's starting to ache, not bad yet, but you know it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the second fix might be harder for machines. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every door frame in a new house is a little bit out, and you have to plane and pack and fiddle until it's right. A machine would need everything perfect. I've never seen a perfect house, and I've seen a lot of houses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ken's roofing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roofs are hard for robots, I think, all that height and weather. But if the building firms build fewer houses because things are uncertain, Ken gets less work too. When building slows, we both feel it at the same time.

S1.say: People need to stop waiting for someone to save them and get on with it. Learn the new things, work hard and look after your own.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried, because I'm the slowest on the gang and a machine could make the others fast enough not to need me. But I think finishing work is harder for machines than people think.
S1.do: Learns new tools once others on site use them, with her daughter's help on the phone side. Saves a bit more, aiming for 30 a week in Ken's good summers, and asks the foreman what skills the firm wants.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a tooth that's starting to ache.
S1.quote: A machine would need everything perfect. I've never seen a perfect house, and I've seen a lot of houses now.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is about self-reliance, while privately she worries about being the slowest on the gang. She takes comfort in how imperfect real houses are. Both household incomes depend on the building trade, which comes up as her deeper concern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and somebody needs to put the brakes on. Even me, and I don't usually want the government sticking its nose in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm terrified. Ken and I are both in building, we've got three weeks in the bank, and if robots can do hands-on work in two years, both of us are out at once. There's no other trade in the house to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything the first month, the phones, the kids' clubs, the meat. I'd ask at church who needs cleaning or childminding, because I can do that, and take any cash work going. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move back near them, though their house is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's falling out of the house. I'd be up every night with the notebook, and the numbers wouldn't add up whichever way I wrote them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with the slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means nothing has time to settle. With the slower one, I'd learn the new tools and get faster, and Ken would still have roofs. With two years, we're both out before I've even finished learning my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't like relying on government. Where would help come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family and church, first. Our church helped the Morrisons when he was ill, food parcels, someone paying the electric. I'd hate to be on the other end of that, but I'd take it before I'd take the government's forms and waiting lists.

S2.say: It's going too fast and somebody needs to put the brakes on. Even me saying that, and I don't usually want the government sticking its nose in.
S2.think: I'm terrified. Ken and I are both in building with three weeks in the bank, so if robots can do hands-on work in two years, we're both out at once with nothing else to fall back on.
S2.do: Cuts phones, the children's clubs and meat in the first month, and looks for cleaning, childminding or cash work through church. Leans on family and church before government, and talks to her parents about moving closer to them.
S2.feel: Like the floor falling out of the house, up every night with numbers that won't add up.
S2.quote: I'd be up every night with the notebook, and the numbers wouldn't add up whichever way I wrote them.
S2.fieldNote: Both incomes depend on building, there are no savings, and she doesn't trust government help, so the fast picture leaves her with no real options. Even so, she wants someone to slow things down, which goes against her usual views. Her plan falls back on cleaning and childminding, the work she did before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of warning if families plan. Don't wait for the government, get ready yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes a real difference. I'd have time to finish my trade and save something, and maybe Ken could move into something steadier. Still scary, but I can work with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, push my door count up and get my skilled card, and save thirty a week. Once others on site are trying the new kit, learn it too. By year three, I'd look at a course in something the machines will need people for, maybe checking finished houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage. Like before a big family Christmas, lots to organise, but you get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you do while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their mum started a new trade at forty and might start another one at forty-six. And that they should work hard at school and learn something useful, a trade or a skill people will always need. And I'd make Joe stop moaning about his homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Emi and Joe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken, honestly. He's stubborn, he's been roofing since he was sixteen. I'd sit him down with the notebook and show him the numbers. He listens to numbers more than he listens to me.

S3.say: Five years is plenty of warning if families plan properly. Don't wait for the government to save you, get ready yourself.
S3.think: Five years makes a real difference, enough time to finish my trade and save something. It's still scary, but I can work with five years.
S3.do: Raises her door count, earns her skilled card and saves 30 a week in the first year. Learns new kit once others try it, and by year three looks at a course in work machines will need people for, such as checking finished houses.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, like organising a big family Christmas.
S3.quote: He listens to numbers more than he listens to me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes her feel she has room to act, and she lays out a clear year-by-year plan. She expects to have to persuade her stubborn husband using the family notebook. Her advice to her children stresses trades and useful skills, fitting her traditional values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to prepare. Families, churches and businesses can sort this out without the government running everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years feels much better. I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, the mortgage much smaller, and I'd have had time to get good at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, get properly skilled at second fix and save steadily. Then, once I see what's working for others, retrain into something the machines can't do, maybe inspecting or teaching apprentices. And make sure the children choose their studies with this in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like something we can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes in your plans compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I wouldn't rush. I'd get really good at my trade first, because skill always counts for something. With five, I'd be learning two things at once, and I'm not built for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Emi wants to do art, and I love that, but I'd want her to have something practical alongside it. Joe likes taking things apart, so maybe he becomes the one who fixes the robots. That would make me laugh.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for anyone to prepare. Families, churches and businesses can sort this out without the government running everything.
S4.think: Ten years feels much better, with the kids grown and the mortgage much smaller. I'd have had time to get good at something.
S4.do: Gets properly skilled at second fix and saves steadily in the early years. Then retrains, once others show what works, into inspecting or teaching apprentices, and steers her children's studies towards practical skills.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, as something the family can plan for.
S4.quote: Joe likes taking things apart, so maybe he becomes the one who fixes the robots. That would make me laugh.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her steady approach fits the timeline, and she would build skill before changing direction. She sees family, church and business as the right answer, not government. Her plans for her children mix pride in their interests with a push towards practical work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt, because Ken and I would both be out at once. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, paid ones, where you learn something new on the job. And some time, honestly, time to pay the mortgage down before it all hits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about couples in the same trade. Everyone says don't put all your eggs in one basket, but when you marry a roofer and work on building sites, the basket is the whole house.

headlineQuote: Everyone says don't put all your eggs in one basket, but when you marry a roofer and work on building sites, the basket is the whole house.
portrait: Carla is a 43-year-old second-fix carpenter on a new housing estate, who came into building at forty after years raising her children and cleaning at a primary school. She keeps the family accounts in a notebook, and with her husband Ken a self-employed roofer, both their incomes depend on building. She is calm in the plateau and uneasy in the steady picture, but panicked by AGI in two years because they would both lose work at once. With five or ten years she becomes a practical planner again, saving and retraining once others show the way. She prefers family, church and business to government help, though the fastest picture shakes that view.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Ken would both lose their building work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships for adults to learn something new on the job, and time to pay down the mortgage before the change hits.
